items.stem: Which term describes a simplified, generalised and often negative image of a group?
items.answer: Stereotype
items.markingKey: Stereotype: a simplified, generalised and often negative image of a group. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “beauty myth”, and give one example.
items.answer: Wolf’s term for the idealised standards of female beauty promoted by the media. Example: airbrushed images of very thin models.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Wolf’s term for the idealised standards of female beauty promoted by the media); 1 mark for a relevant example such as airbrushed images of very thin models. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “hegemonic masculinity” and “heteronormativity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hegemonic masculinity: the dominant, idealised form of masculinity associated with strength, toughness and heterosexuality (e.g. action heroes who never show emotion). Heteronormativity: the assumption that heterosexuality is normal and natural, reflected in media representations (e.g. gay characters shown only as comic sidekicks).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A men’s magazine in Riyadh features a male action star with a muscular body on almost every cover. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the media are part of patriarchal culture: they objectify women, present male dominance as normal and serve men’s interests (Mulvey, Wolf).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A content analysis of adverts on television in Singapore finds that women appear most often in adverts for cleaning products and cosmetics, while men appear in adverts for cars and banking. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: media-saturated society offers endless choice; audiences actively construct identities from media images, and reality and representation blur (Baudrillard, Strinati).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A popular streaming drama made in Lagos features a female police chief, a stay-at-home father and a gay couple raising children. Compare how liberal feminist and postmodernist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: the media reinforce gender stereotypes through socialisation, but representations are improving as more women work in the media (Tuchman, Gauntlett). Postmodernism: media-saturated society offers endless choice; audiences actively construct identities from media images, and reality and representation blur (Baudrillard, Strinati).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research the roles given to men and women in television adverts.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; positivists see them as objective “social facts” that can be used to test hypotheses. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the roles given to men and women in television adverts but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying the roles given to men and women in television adverts.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the roles given to men and women in television adverts but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “male gaze” and “symbolic annihilation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Male gaze: Mulvey’s term for the way the camera presents women as sexual objects from a heterosexual male viewpoint (e.g. camera lingering on a female character’s body). Symbolic annihilation: Tuchman’s term for the absence, condemnation or trivialisation of women in the media (e.g. few female experts interviewed on news).

items.stem: Grace, a sociology student, is designing a project on how teenage girls respond to images of models on social media. Explain one strength and two limitations of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strength: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences. Limitations: 1. the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear. 2. they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare.
items.markingKey: For each of three points: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how teenage girls respond to images of models on social media. [6]

items.stem: Industry data and a content analysis of television programmes are shown below. Table: percentage of women | 2005 | 2022. Speaking characters who are women | 37% | 43%. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media representations of women are improving.
items.answer: (a) 27 − 19 = +8 percentage points. items.stem: Distinguish between “tokenism” and “Orientalism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Tokenism: including a small number of minority characters to appear diverse without real representation (e.g. one minority character in an otherwise white cast). items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how older people feel about the way the media represent them.
items.answer: Strengths: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups; response rates are usually higher than for postal questionnaires because the interviewer is present. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how older people feel about the way the media represent them but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research how disabled characters are represented in films.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how disabled characters are represented in films but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using laboratory experiments to research how disabled people feel about their representation in the media.
items.answer: Strengths: the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified; the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; participants who know they are being studied may change their behaviour (the Hawthorne effect or demand characteristics). Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how disabled people feel about their representation in the media but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.markingKey: Male gaze: Mulvey’s term for the way the camera presents women as sexual objects from a heterosexual male viewpoint. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “male gaze”.
items.answer: Mulvey’s term for the way the camera presents women as sexual objects from a heterosexual male viewpoint.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Mulvey’s term for the way the camera presents women as sexual objects from a heterosexual male viewpoint. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Tuchman used the term symbolic annihilation to describe the absence and trivialisation of women in the media.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It refers to women being ignored, condemned or trivialised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which the media may stereotype women.
items.answer: Symbolic annihilation (absence, trivialisation); domestic and caring roles; sexual objectification (male gaze); beauty myth; focus on appearance rather than achievements.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: A content analysis of television in a country near Riyadh produced the results below. Table: percentage of women | 2005 | 2022. Speaking characters who are women | 31% | 37%. News experts interviewed who are women | 25% | 33%. Directors who are women | 10% | 18%. By how many percentage points did the figure for News experts interviewed who are women change between 2005 and 2022?
items.answer: +8 percentage points
items.markingKey: 33 − 25 = +8 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Industry data and a content analysis of television programmes are shown below. Table: percentage of women | 2005 | 2022. Speaking characters who are women | 33% | 36%. News experts interviewed who are women | 19% | 29%. Directors who are women | 9% | 14%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Speaking characters who are women between 2005 and 2022. (b) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) 36 − 33 = +3 percentage points. (b) The figure rose for Speaking characters who are women, News experts interviewed who are women, Directors who are women; Speaking characters who are women had the highest figure for 2022.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 33 and 36; 1 mark for +3 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: A content analysis of television in a country near Istanbul produced the results below. Table: percentage of women | 2005 | 2022. Speaking characters who are women | 35% | 45%. News experts interviewed who are women | 19% | 27%. Directors who are women | 10% | 14%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Speaking characters who are women between 2005 and 2022. (b) Calculate the gap between Speaking characters who are women and Directors who are women in 2005 and in 2022, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (c) Describe two patterns shown in the data.
items.answer: (a) 45 − 35 = +10 percentage points. (b) 2005: 25 percentage points; 2022: 31 percentage points; the gap widened. (c) The figure rose for Speaking characters who are women, News experts interviewed who are women, Directors who are women; Speaking characters who are women had the highest figure for 2022.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 35 and 45; 1 mark for +10 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) 1 mark each gap (25 and 31); 1 mark for “widened”. [3] (c) 1 mark for each accurate pattern supported by figures from the table. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying how teenage girls respond to images of models on social media.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teenage girls respond to images of models on social media but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: To what extent do sociological arguments and evidence support the view that media representations of gender continue to reinforce traditional stereotypes?
items.answer: For: Tuchman, Mulvey, Wolf; content analyses of adverts and news; beauty myth on social media; hegemonic masculinity. Against: Gauntlett: more diverse identities; strong female leads; changing masculinities; active audiences; self-representation on social media; postmodern choice. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Tuchman, Mulvey, Wolf; content analyses of adverts and news; beauty myth on social media; hegemonic masculinity. Against: Gauntlett: more diverse identities; strong female leads; changing masculinities; active audiences; self-representation on social media; postmodern choice. [12]

items.stem: Which term describes including a small number of minority characters to appear diverse without real representation?
items.answer: Tokenism
items.markingKey: Tokenism: including a small number of minority characters to appear diverse without real representation. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “demonisation”.
items.answer: Presenting a group as evil or a threat to society.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: presenting a group as evil or a threat to society. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which the media may represent ethnic minorities stereotypically.
items.answer: As a threat (crime, terrorism); as a problem (immigration); exotic or Orientalist images; tokenism; absence (symbolic annihilation); limited roles.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: Mohammed carried out a content analysis of TV drama and news in a country where 14% of people are from minority ethnic groups. Table: percentage of characters in each type of role who are from minority ethnic groups | 2010 | 2022. Leading roles | 7% | 11%. Criminal roles | 26% | 17%. News experts | 5% | 10%. By how many percentage points did the figure for News experts change between 2010 and 2022?
items.answer: +5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 10 − 5 = +5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, is designing a project on how older people feel about the way the media represent them. Explain one limitation of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: The researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how older people feel about the way the media represent them. [2]

items.stem: Freya, a sociology student, is designing a project on how older people feel about the way the media represent them. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: results are quantitative and easy to compare; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: it would be unethical to recreate harmful situations, such as violence, in a laboratory; many social issues cannot be studied in a laboratory for ethical or practical reasons. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how older people feel about the way the media represent them but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the view that people are disabled by barriers and attitudes in society rather than by their impairments?
items.answer: Social model of disability
items.markingKey: Social model of disability: the view that people are disabled by barriers and attitudes in society rather than by their impairments. [1]

items.stem: Explain two stereotypes of disabled people identified in media research.
items.answer: Pitiable and pathetic; sinister or evil (villains); supercrip; burden; object of curiosity; incapable of relationships (Barnes).
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained stereotype. [4]

items.stem: A charity advert in Singapore shows a disabled child alone in a dark room with sad music and the words “Without you, she has no future.” Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: media labels and stereotypes of disabled people shape how others see them and how they see themselves (Barnes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Amara, a sociology student, is designing a project on how disabled people feel about their representation in the media. Explain two strengths of using participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. It reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens. 2. It is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how disabled people feel about their representation in the media. [4]

items.stem: (a) Explain two stereotypes of disabled people in the media. (b) “Media representations of disabled people reinforce negative stereotypes.” Evaluate this view.
items.answer: (a) Pitiable; sinister; supercrip; burden; incapable of relationships; comic figure; medical-model focus. (b) For: Barnes’s stereotypes; under-representation; charity imagery; disability as plot device (Shakespeare); medical model framing. Against: Paralympics coverage; disabled actors and presenters; social model campaigns; social media self-representation; improving but uneven. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
